newsitem.title: USA: Profiles of the leaders at the Denver G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Profiles of the leaders at the Denver G7 summit.

text.p: The world leaders meeting at the G7 summit in Denver this week have learned the common lesson that radical solutions to their domestic political problems will not wash with voters.

The only new face at the Group of Seven leader's table will be Britain's Tony Blair, who cut the socialist teeth from his Labour Party and dragged it to the centre of British politics to end 18 years of Conservative Party rule in May.

France's President Jacques Chirac returns a shrunken figure from the brash, ebullient conservative who shouldered his way to centre stage at the Halifax summit two years ago and revelled in the host's role at Lyon last summer.

His political judgment is suspect after his gamble to call an early election in which the French people thunderously rejected his attempt to slash back the welfare state, electing left-leaning centrist Lionel Jospin as his prime minister.
Brief profiles of the leaders:

U.S. PRESIDENT BILL CLINTON, 50, strides into the Denver meeting as not just the leader of the world's most powerful country but one whose economic policy is held up as a model in recovering from the fiscal laxity of the 1980s.

In what one analyst described as a "gold era for the U.S. economy", unemployment is at its lowest level in nearly 24 years, the government budget deficit is small and shrinking, and inflation is low and stable.

In the first year of his second and last term, Clinton comes unencumbered with re-election pressures. Although it has not affected his high approval ratings, he is surrounded by a haze of scandal, with investigations underway of charges of improper fund-raising, abuse of power and sexual harassment.
Clinton is struggling in two of his top foreign policy aims, nailing down a lasting peace in the Middle East and helping impose order in the Balkans, issues that will be raised at Denver.

GERMAN CHANCELLOR HELMUT KOHL, 67, is attending his 15th G7 summit. But Kohl, who after German unification in 1990 dominated such international meetings, will go to Denver weaker than at any time in the past.
In a major embarrassment, his government looks set to miss the strict criteria for Europe's single currency -- criteria he helped write.

The conservative Kohl, who faces an election next year, is is under pressure after election successes of left-wing parties in Britain and France. He will have to deal carefully with a planned jobs initiative that Clinton and Blair want to launch in Denver, an idea he has resisted for Europe.

FRENCH PRESIDENT JACQUES CHIRAC, 64, goes to Denver with his power gutted by left-wing victory in a parliamentary election. He must share power in foreign affairs and defence with new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and forfeit almost all say over economic and trade policy.

He brings perhaps the worst economic record of the G7 -- sluggish growth, heavy taxes and the highest unemployment rate in the G7 at 12.8 percent, all of which played a key role in the electoral defeat of Chirac's centre-right coalition.
Jospin, who will not be in Denver, has vowed to give jobs priority over austerity, reversing the Chirac stand.
G7 leaders would be unwise to write Chirac off. He can dissolve parliament again once the new legislature has run a year and his seven-year term does not expire until 2002.

BRITISH PRIME MINISTER TONY BLAIR, 44, breezes into the G7 club from a country euphoric after years of increasingly unpopular Conservative rule ended in last month's election. At home he can do no wrong -- even triumphs by English cricket and soccer teams have been jokingly ascribed to his influence.

A committed Christian dubbed "Bambi" for his squeaky-clean image and Tony Blur for his tendency to waffle, he is seen as a pragmatic centrist, dedicated to bringing "opportunity to all (Britain's) people and not merely a limited number."

He has shown respect but no obsequiousness to more experienced European leaders, telling them they must shake up their ideas to tackle mass unemployment. He has promised a new start in relations with Europe, looking for cooperation after the confrontational tone set by Margaret Thatcher.
After an affable meeting with Clinton in London last month he launched a joint initiative to put "employability" at the top of the G7 agenda for the next two years.

ITALIAN PRIME MINISTER ROMANO PRODI, 57, a centrist economist who heads a centre-left coalition government, is now starting his second year in office, a feat that makes him one of few Italian leaders to attend successive G7 summits. Italy has had 55 governments since World War Two.

A former chairman of Italian state industrial holding IRI, Prodi has put the emphasis of his premierhip on lowering Italy's high budget deficits and taming inflation. He has vowed to resign if Italy fails to make membership of Europe's single currency in the first wave.

He will be in Denver looking for appreciation of his economic policy and action on jobs as he prepares to enter difficult negotiations with trade unions and hard-left allies on reform of the welfare state, a key challenge in Italy's bid to sustain single currency criteria.
CANADIAN PRIME MINISTER JEAN CHRETIEN, 63, comes fresh from re-election to a second mandate, although his Liberals saw their majority shaved to a paper-thin 155 of 301 seats.

Chretien is a veteran of three decades in politics whose ideology has vacillated with the times, from big spender in the 1970s to fiscal tightwad in the 1990s as he had to rein in unsustainable deficits.
He delights in saying his policies are in the "radical center" between left and right. His rivals in the campaign said he displayed little vision for Canada's future.
It will be his fourth G7 summit. He hosted the 1995 Halifax meeting. Chretien will want to highlight his country's improved public finances.

JAPANESE PRIME MINISTER RYUTARO HASHIMOTO, 59, who practices mediaeval swordsmanship for a hobby, is engaged in a sweeping reform of social, economic and financial systems to try to open up Japan to free competition.

A veteran politician with a sometimes abrupt manner, he earned an international reputation in his former role of trade minister when he was an obdurate defender of national interests, particularly in talks with the United States.
He is likely to come under questioning from other leaders over Japan's growing trade surplus and a series of financial scandals and may be pressured to speed up domestic reforms.

Japanese officials say Hashimoto hopes to give Japan a higher profile at his second G7 summit with proposals on global issues like promoting development in Africa and on anti-terrorism, nuclear energy safety and the environment.
Hashimoto will be carrying the banner for Asia in what is shaping up as a Euro-centric conference.

PRESIDENT BORIS YELTSIN, 66, has thrust himself back to the helm of Russian politics after a near-death experience physically and politically last year when he scraped through a presidential election and and underwent open heart surgery. He still enjoys the support of G7 leaders as standard bearer for Russian reform.
Yeltsin, who missed last year's summit because of illness, will take part in all but one of the meetings -- an hour-long session on economic and financial issues.
U.S. officials say Russia's expanded role at Denver is justified by its weight in the world and its presence serves the interests of top industrial nations, as well as Russia itself.

Yeltsin will be seeking as big a role as possible for Russia at the meetings but he is hampered by Moscow's deep economic depression and huge problems transforming itself from a communist state into a free market economy.
